p: Our class did a clean up at the beach. We found bottles, bags and straws. We put them all in the bin so the turtles stay safe.
At home we have three bins. One is for rubbish, one is for recycling and one is for garden waste. I help sort the rubbish.

s: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system in the world.
Reduce, reuse and recycle are three ways to cut down on waste.
Soft plastics can be recycled at special bins in some supermarkets.
Food scraps in landfill create a gas that warms the planet.
Planting native trees gives local birds and insects a place to live.
Electric cars produce no exhaust fumes while they are driving.
Our school reduced its paper use by sharing files online.

Turning off appliances at the wall saves electricity.

We wrote letters asking the canteen to stop using plastic straws.

p: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the coast of Queensland for more than two thousand kilometres. It is home to fish, turtles, dolphins and many kinds of coral. Warmer oceans, pollution and storms can damage the reef. Scientists and rangers work hard to protect it for the future.

Our class decided to reduce the rubbish in our lunch boxes. For one week, we counted every piece of packaging we threw away. Then we tried a nude food day, with no plastic wrappers at all. By the end of the month, our class rubbish had dropped by half.

Plastic does not break down like food or paper. Instead, it breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics. These pieces can end up in rivers and oceans, where fish and birds swallow them. Using fewer single-use plastics is an easy way to help.

Composting turns food scraps and garden waste into rich soil. Worms, bacteria and fungi break down the waste over a few weeks. Compost helps plants grow and reduces the amount of rubbish sent to landfill. It is a simple way to help the environment at home.

Solar panels collect energy from the sun and turn it into electricity. Many Australian homes have solar panels on their roofs because we get lots of sunshine. Using solar power reduces the need to burn coal, which releases pollution into the air.

Wetlands are areas of land covered by shallow water, such as swamps and marshes. They act like natural sponges, soaking up floodwater and filtering pollution. Many birds visit wetlands to feed and breed. Some birds fly all the way from Siberia to Australian wetlands every year.

s: Sustainability means meeting our needs today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, causing the planet's average temperature to rise.
Australia has some of the highest rates of household waste per person in the world.
A circular economy designs products so that materials can be reused rather than thrown away.
Mangrove forests protect coastlines from erosion and act as nurseries for young fish.
Overfishing can reduce fish populations faster than they are able to recover.
Fast fashion encourages people to buy cheap clothing that is quickly discarded.
Land clearing for agriculture remains a major cause of habitat loss in Australia.
Electronic waste contains valuable metals that can be recovered through recycling.
Energy-efficient buildings use insulation, shading and natural light to reduce power use.
Some cities now collect food waste separately to turn it into compost or energy.
Marine parks restrict fishing and other activities to protect ocean ecosystems.
Carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are higher now than at any time in human history.
Reusing a product often saves more energy than recycling it.
Stormwater carries litter, oil and chemicals from streets directly into creeks and bays.
Native plants usually need less water and fertiliser than introduced garden species.
Young people around the world have organised climate strikes to call for urgent action.
Deforestation reduces the number of trees available to absorb carbon dioxide.
Water-sensitive urban design captures and cleans rainwater before it reaches waterways.
Recycling only works when people sort their waste correctly and avoid contamination.
Australia's Murray-Darling Basin supplies water to farms, towns and ecosystems across four states.
Buying locally grown food can reduce the emissions created by transporting goods long distances.
Bushcare groups remove weeds and replant native species in local reserves.
Light pollution can disrupt the behaviour of nocturnal animals and migrating birds.
Individual actions matter, but large-scale change also requires government and business action.
p: Climate change refers to long-term changes in global temperatures and weather patterns. Since the industrial revolution, burning coal, oil and gas has released large amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. This gas traps heat, gradually warming the planet. Effects include more extreme heatwaves, rising sea levels and changes to rainfall, which affect people, farms and natural ecosystems.

A circular economy aims to eliminate waste by keeping products and materials in use for as long as possible. Instead of the traditional pattern of take, make and throw away, items are designed to be repaired, shared, reused and eventually recycled. Some companies now offer repair services or take back old products so their materials can be used again.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees that grow along tropical and subtropical coastlines. Their tangled roots trap sediment, protecting the shore from erosion and storm damage. They also provide shelter for young fish, crabs and prawns. Mangroves store large amounts of carbon in their soil, making them important in the fight against climate change, yet they are often cleared for development.

The Murray-Darling Basin is Australia's largest river system and one of its most important farming regions. Water from the rivers is used for crops, livestock and towns, but taking too much can harm the environment. During droughts, fish deaths and poor water quality have highlighted the challenge of sharing water fairly between farmers, communities and the ecosystems that depend on it.

Recycling can reduce waste, but it is not a perfect solution. When non-recyclable items are placed in recycling bins, they contaminate the whole load, sometimes sending it to landfill. Some materials, such as certain plastics, have few buyers and are difficult to recycle. That is why experts emphasise reducing and reusing first, with recycling as the final option.

Many students are taking action on environmental issues in their own communities. Some have organised campaigns to remove single-use plastics from canteens, while others have planted trees or monitored water quality in local creeks. These projects show that young people can make real change. They also help students develop skills in research, communication and leadership.

s: Limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius would require rapid and far-reaching transitions across every sector of the economy.
Australia's heavy reliance on coal exports places it in a difficult position as global demand for fossil fuels declines.
Carbon offsets remain controversial because some projects may not deliver the emissions reductions they claim.
The concept of planetary boundaries identifies limits within which humanity can safely operate.
Environmental justice highlights how pollution and climate impacts often fall hardest on disadvantaged communities.
Green hydrogen produced with renewable electricity could help decarbonise heavy industry and shipping.
Biodiversity loss and climate change are interconnected crises that must be addressed together.
Extended producer responsibility makes manufacturers accountable for the disposal of their products.
Land rights and native title have given Traditional Owners a stronger voice in managing country.
Critics of geoengineering warn that technological fixes could distract from the need to cut emissions.
The true cost of goods rarely reflects the environmental damage caused during their production.
Regenerative agriculture seeks to restore soil health while maintaining productive farming systems.
Climate litigation is increasingly used to hold governments and corporations accountable for environmental harm.
A just transition aims to support workers and communities that depend on fossil fuel industries.
Ocean acidification threatens shell-forming organisms as seawater absorbs more carbon dioxide.
Effective environmental policy must balance economic growth, social wellbeing and ecological limits.
Greenwashing occurs when companies exaggerate the environmental benefits of their products or practices.
Rewilding and habitat restoration can deliver benefits for biodiversity, water quality and carbon storage.
Consumption patterns in wealthy nations contribute disproportionately to global environmental pressures.
Critical minerals such as lithium are essential for batteries, yet mining them carries environmental costs.
Intergenerational equity asks whether current generations have the right to deplete resources needed by future ones.
Australia has committed to reaching net zero emissions by 2050, though the pathway remains debated.
Urban planning that prioritises walking, cycling and public transport can substantially reduce emissions.
Scientific uncertainty about specific impacts should not be confused with uncertainty about the overall direction of change.
Collective action problems arise when individuals benefit from others' sacrifices without contributing themselves.
p: The idea of a just transition recognises that moving away from fossil fuels will affect workers and regions differently. Towns built around coal mines or power stations face the loss of well-paid jobs and the businesses that depend on them. Advocates argue that governments should plan ahead, investing in retraining programs, new industries and infrastructure so that communities are not left behind. Without such planning, resistance to climate policy is likely to grow, slowing the transition for everyone.

Greenwashing describes the practice of making misleading claims about the environmental benefits of a product, service or company. Labels such as eco-friendly or carbon neutral may sound reassuring but are sometimes vague or unsupported by evidence. Regulators in Australia have begun investigating and penalising misleading claims. Consumers can protect themselves by looking for independent certification and asking how a claim has been measured, verified and reported over time.

Australia's position as a major exporter of coal and gas creates a complex dilemma. These industries generate significant revenue and employment, yet their products contribute to global emissions when burned overseas. As trading partners commit to reducing emissions, demand for these exports is expected to decline. Some economists argue Australia could become a renewable energy superpower, exporting green hydrogen, critical minerals and clean manufactured goods, but realising this vision requires substantial investment and long-term policy certainty.

Biodiversity loss is sometimes overshadowed by climate change, yet scientists warn it is an equally serious crisis. Healthy ecosystems provide clean water, pollination, fertile soils and protection from natural hazards, services that economies depend upon. Australia has listed hundreds of species as threatened, and recovery plans are often underfunded. Integrating biodiversity into decisions about land use, infrastructure and agriculture is increasingly seen as essential rather than optional.

Traditional Owners have cared for country across the Australian continent for more than sixty thousand years. Their knowledge of fire, water and seasonal change is increasingly recognised in environmental management. Indigenous ranger programs employ people to protect cultural sites, manage feral animals and conduct cultural burns. These programs deliver environmental benefits while strengthening communities and cultural identity, demonstrating how social and ecological goals can be achieved together.

Individual choices, such as eating less meat or flying less often, can reduce a person's environmental footprint. However, some argue that focusing on individual responsibility distracts attention from the structural changes required, including regulation of major polluters and investment in public infrastructure. In reality, both levels matter. Personal choices can shift social norms and markets, while policy changes make sustainable options easier, cheaper and more accessible for everyone.
